description:
The Town council approved the ordinance on first reading at their August 19, 2026 Town Council Meeting. The Town does not produce its own drinking water. Instead, it purchases treated water in bulk from Miami-Dade County and resells it to homes and businesses through the Water Fund. In a letter dated July 8, 2026, the County notified the Town that wholesale water rates will increase by 4.3% for FY 2026–2027, from $2.4678 to $2.5731 per 1,000 gallons. Staff's analysis assumes that County increases of a similar size (approximately 4% annually) are expected to continue in future years.
In addition to rising wholesale costs, the Water Fund's day-to-day operating expenses including salaries, supplies, equipment, and maintenance—have outpaced revenues, creating a widening structural gap. Operating losses grew from approximately $23,600 in FY2024 to $94,400 in FY2025. This shortfall has been covered by drawing down available reserves, which is not sustainable long-term.
The Water Fund must also finance two upcoming infrastructure projects:
BLK 11 Alleyway Water Main Replacement (near Town Hall): Estimated $1.2 million (FY2027–FY2028);
NE 96th Street Water Main Replacement: Estimated $63,500 (FY2029).
The Water Fund has no outstanding debt; accordingly, these projects are planned to be paid for directly from rates and reserves rather than through borrowing. The Town may pursue grant funding to help offset the BLK 11 project cost; none is assumed in this analysis, so any grant awarded would be a benefit beyond what is shown here.
Staff has projected revenues and anticipated expenses including capital spending and we recommend a 5.0% increase for FY27. The FY27 increase along with planned future increases will:
Cover the rising wholesale cost of water purchased from Miami-Dade County;
Fund both planned water infrastructure projects without new borrowing;
Eliminate the operating deficit; and
Maintain reserves at or above 25% annual operating cost.

As with any 75-year-old bridge that is in a corrosive environment, constant repairs and maintenance are required to keep the structure in safe operating condition. Item # 4 in Table # 1 addressed header joint repairs. Out of nineteen joint (19) repairs that were completed in that PO, eight (8) had to be reworked. The cause of failure of the eight reworked repairs was that concrete deterioration was continuous from top to bottom of the deck slabs and extended considerable distances from the slab edges. The replacement concrete of the reworked repairs had no structurally sound concrete to adhere to and collapsed.
Repair Options
The new bridge is expected to be commissioned in 2032-2034, and therefore the existing bridge is required to stay in service for another 6-8 years. The selected repair option shall therefore represent an optimal mix of longevity and costs. The following repair options were considered:
Remove and replace weakened concrete associated with the header joints. This will be very costly because of the volume of deteriorated concrete that must be replaced. This option is cost prohibitive with no guarantee of success, since the full extent of compromised concrete has not been determined. This option may also require prolonged lane/bridge closures.
Modular expansion joint systems may be used to replace deficient joints, but this option is also expensive with no guarantee of success, as it is dependent on attaching the new jointing system to structurally sound concrete. This option may also require prolonged lane/bridge closures.
Utilize 5/8” thick steel plates to go over deficient joints and distribute traffic loads to deck slab concrete that is structurally sound. This option will not require prolonged lane/bridge closures.
Of the three, option number 3 is by far the cheapest since it does not require removal and replacement of weakened concrete at the header joints. Although it is not a permanent repair like the other two, it is expected to last for 6-8 years or until the bridge is decommissioned.
DISCUSSION
To avoid delays and to undertake the necessary work before the re-opening of school in August 2026, the Town Manager authorized Florida Draw Bridges Inc. (FDI) on 6 July 2026 to begin work. FDI requires a lead time of about 2 weeks to procure materials.
This temporary repair methodology for deteriorated expansion (header) joints was used successfully on the Venetian Causeway, and photographs of the finished work are attached.

BACKGROUND
Miami Dade Conty Code (MDCC) requires that Volume Sewer Customers (VSC) of the Miami Dade Water and Sewer Department (MDWSD) comply with the threshold for infiltration and Inflow (I/I) of 5,000 gallon per day-inch-mile (GPDIM). When Cycle 3 Phase 1 Sanitary Sewer Evaluation Survey (SSES) was submitted by Hazen and Sawyer to the Miami Dade Department of Environmental Resources Management (DERM) on November 12, 2022, three (of the six) sewer sub basins were found to be out of compliance. In conjunction with the Public Works Department, a corrective action plan (CAP) was developed by Hazen and Sawyer to bring these basins into compliance.
INTRODUCTION
At the 22 April 2026 regular Council meeting Council approved a contract with Hazen and Sawyer to provide engineering services to submit the SSES Cycle 3 Phase 1 RFI and Phase 2 regulatory report to (DERM). These submissions are due by 12 November 2026, and failure to timely submit reports or submit reports that illustrate one or more of the sewage collection basins are not in compliance with the threshold for infiltration and Inflow (I/I), will result in a temporary sewer moratorium placed for the non-compliant basin(s).
To show compliance with the threshold for all sub basins, DERM requires flow monitoring and measurements during the wet season of June 1 to November 30, 2026. The proposal from CMA includes the installation of nine (9) flow meters to obtain the flow data.
DISCUSSION
CMA has contracted with a sub-consultant called ADS Environmental Services (ADS) to perform flow monitoring and measurements. ADS is a reputable firm who has worked with the Town before, and who has the expertise to undertake sewage flow monitoring and measurements. A contract amendment was executed to include ADS as a nominated sub consultant with CMA.

description:
Discussion and possible action to authorize the Town Manager to close twelve (12) Town bank accounts maintained at Bank of America, as listed herein, maintaining the General Fund account ending in 0007 (which will serve as the master Treasury Fund) and the Accounts Payable clearing account ending in 1644, and to transfer remaining balances to the Treasury Fund, except for two pension accounts whose funds will be transferred to The Florida Municipal Pension Trust Fund (FMPTF).
BACKGROUND:
At the January 14, 2026 meeting, the Town Council authorized the Town Manager to procure OpenGov’s ERP suite, including Financial Management, Budgeting, and Utility Billing modules. As part of the ongoing implementation and system configuration, the Town is transitioning to a pooled-cash architecture. Under this setup, a master Treasury Fund holds all non-invested operating cash in a single account, while individual fund equity and interest earnings are tracked via general ledger accounting. The Town's existing General Fund account (ending in 0007) will serve as this master Treasury Fund.
Interest earned on pooled cash will be allocated proportionally to the participating funds based on their respective equity balances.
Currently, the Town utilizes the General Fund as an operational clearing account for nearly all financial activity. Expenditures and revenues for distinct funds (e.g., the Causeway Fund) pass through the General Fund, generating extensive interfund payables and receivables. Implementing the pooled-cash Treasury Fund will eliminate these repetitive interfund clearing transactions and simplify cash management by drastically reducing the number of external bank accounts required.
Statutory & Accounting Compliance for Restricted Funds
This pooled-cash structure fully complies with relevant Florida Statutes, IRS regulations, and Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB) guidelines regarding accounting for restricted funds:
Impact Fees: Governed by the Florida Impact Fee Act (§ 163.31801, F.S.) and Municipal Home Rule Authority (§ 166.04151, F.S.).
Building Permit Fees: Authorized under Municipal Fee Authority (§ 166.222, F.S.) and governed by the Florida Building Code framework (§ 553.80(7), F.S.), which mandates permit and inspection fee tracking and reporting.
Future Bond Proceeds: When and if the Town issues bonds in the future, proceeds will be maintained in a separate, dedicated bank account to ensure strict compliance with IRS regulations (including arbitrage restrictions) and specific bond covenants.
Separate ledger accounting fulfills statutory obligations for general operating and restricted fee resources; these do not require physical placement in separate bank accounts. In accordance with the Florida Department of Financial Services (DFS) Uniform Accounting System Manual and GASB Codification Section 1300.119, separate funds serve to identify and segregate assets, liabilities, revenues, and expenditures in the ledger, but do not require physical segregation of bank deposits. Maintaining self-balancing sets of ledger accounts within the ERP ensures legal and operational compliance.
Implementation Action & Specific Accounts
Advance authorization is requested to close the unnecessary Bank of America accounts while system configuration is completed. The following twelve (12) bank accounts will be closed:
Operating & Capital Accounts (Balances transferred to General Fund/Treasury Fund 0007):Parking Meter Fund (ending in 1719)
Broad Causeway Revenue Fund (ending in 1727)
General Capital Fund (ending in 2176)
Water Fund (ending in 2184)
Payroll Clearing (ending in 0015)
Customer Deposits (ending in 6621)
Sewer Account (ending in 0057)
Solid Waste Fund (ending in 4188)
Stormwater Fund (ending in 4615)
Law Enforcement Trust Fund (ending in 0852)
Pension Accounts (Balances transferred to FMPTF):Employees Retirement System (ending in 0073)
Employees Retirement System (ending in 7408)
Note on Pension Accounts: These two Employees Retirement System accounts consist of Chapter 185 insurance premium tax distributions dating back to prior to FY 2016, along with associated interest. The premium tax is collected by the State of Florida on certain property and casualty insurance policies covering properties within the Town of Bay Harbor Islands and remitted to the Town. These funds are distributed to eligible local governments to provide supplemental pension benefits for police officers. The funds were remitted to the Town and deposited into these Bank of America accounts but were never transferred to the pension administrator. These monies are included in the cash balance of the pension fund and are not considered Town funds; closing the accounts and transferring the balances directly to The Florida Municipal Pension Trust Fund (FMPTF) resolves this long-standing administrative item.
Retained Bank Accounts:General Fund Account (ending in 0007) – To serve as the Treasury Fund
Accounts Payable Clearing Account (ending in 1644)

description:
The Town does not produce its own drinking water. Instead, it purchases treated water in bulk from Miami-Dade County and resells it to homes and businesses through the Water Fund. In a letter dated July 8, 2026, the County notified the Town that wholesale water rates will increase by 4.3% for FY 2026–2027, from $2.4678 to $2.5731 per 1,000 gallons. Staff's analysis assumes that County increases of a similar size (approximately 4% annually) are expected to continue in future years.
In addition to rising wholesale costs, the Water Fund's day-to-day operating expenses including salaries, supplies, equipment, and maintenance—have outpaced revenues, creating a widening structural gap. Operating losses grew from approximately $23,600 in FY2024 to $94,400 in FY2025. This shortfall has been covered by drawing down available reserves, which is not sustainable long-term.
The Water Fund must also finance two upcoming infrastructure projects:
BLK 11 Alleyway Water Main Replacement (near Town Hall): Estimated $1.2 million (FY2027–FY2028);
NE 96th Street Water Main Replacement: Estimated $63,500 (FY2029).
The Water Fund has no outstanding debt; accordingly, these projects are planned to be paid for directly from rates and reserves rather than through borrowing. The Town may pursue grant funding to help offset the BLK 11 project cost; none is assumed in this analysis, so any grant awarded would be a benefit beyond what is shown here.
Staff has projected revenues and anticipated expenses including capital spending and we recommend a 5.0% increase for FY27. The FY27 increase along with planned future increases will:
Cover the rising wholesale cost of water purchased from Miami-Dade County;
Fund both planned water infrastructure projects without new borrowing;
Eliminate the operating deficit; and
Maintain reserves at or above 25% annual operating cost.

description:
The Town owns and operates the Broad Causeway, which connects Bay Harbor Islands to the mainland. The Town currently offers two toll pass plans available to any person on request, with no residency or other eligibility restrictions. Passes are issued on a rolling basis, with terms measured from the date of issuance.
Staff is requesting Council consideration and direction regarding three proposed options for the Broad Causeway pass plan program:
Option 1: Five-category eligibility structure with a two-tier pricing model ($200/$150 for residents, $350/$225 standard).
Option 2: Restrict eligibility strictly to Bay Harbor Islands residents (vehicles registered in Bay Harbor Islands only) at $200 for an annual pass and $150 for a six-month pass.
Option 3: Allow certain proximity residents in designated areas to obtain a pass if the Town reaches reciprocal agreements with those areas providing appropriate benefits/concessions to Bay Harbor Islands residents, using a base price of $350/$225 with a $150/$75 rebate for Bay Harbor Islands residents.
CURRENT PROGRAM OVERVIEW The Town currently offers two toll pass plans with the following terms and pricing:

PROGRAM OPTIONS FOR COUNCIL CONSIDERATION
OPTION 1: Five-Category Eligibility & Two-Tier Pricing Structure
Restricts eligibility for the annual and six-month Broad Causeway pass plans to five designated categories with standard and discounted resident rates:
Category 1: Residents
Individuals whose primary legal residence is within the corporate limits of the Town of Bay Harbor Islands. (Eligible for a discounted resident rate: $200 Annual / $150 Six-Month.)

Category 3: Employees

Category 4: School Families

Category 5: Proximity Residents - Designated Areas
Individuals whose primary legal residence is located within designated municipalities or neighborhoods: Bal Harbour, Indian Creek Village, Surfside, San Souci, and Keystone Point. (Standard rate applies: $350 Annual / $225 Six-Month.)

LEGAL AUTHORITY Staff reviewed the applicable legal framework and referred the matter to the Town Attorney for an opinion.
Research Conducted by Staff
Special Act: Staff reviewed the 1947 special act of the Florida Legislature authorizing the causeway. No prohibition on resident-exclusive toll rates or pass plan eligibility was found.
Bond Indentures: The causeway debt was refinanced in 2003 and again in 2012. Current note documents contain no restriction preventing resident-exclusive rates or pass eligibility restrictions.
2016 Council Discussion: A prior Town Attorney was asked whether the Town could offer a partial refund to residents after the fact, a question about a rebate, not a pre-set discount at the point of sale. That question was not resolved at the meeting and does not speak to the present proposal.
Opinion of the Town Attorney
After reviewing the special act, current bond documents, and relevant history, the Town Attorney concluded that the Town has the legal authority to create its own resident toll program, similar to Miami-Dade County’s residential toll program for Key Biscayne. The Town may lawfully restrict pass plan eligibility to the proposed categories.

description:
Background
In April 1998, the Town entered into a revolving loan agreement with the State of Florida Department of Environmental Protection to finance the planning and design of a sewer rehabilitation and replacement project. Debt service payments for this State Revolving Fund Loan were collateralized by the net revenues of the Town's sewer system.

We are requesting authorization to transfer residual funds totaling approximately $105,295 from the sewer debt service bank account into the primary Sewer Fund bank account. Furthermore, we request authorization to officially close the sewer debt service bank account.

attachments.name: MEMO TO APPROVE BCC TO REHABILITATE BRIDGE # 875105 V3

description:
PREAMBLE
In 2002 FDOT informed the Town that the West Relief Bridge was severely compromised and must be posted for weight restrictions not exceeding 2 Tons. This restriction was so severe that it prohibited any vehicle that was heavier than a car from crossing the bridge. Kimley Horn and Associates (KHA), one of the Town’s CCNA consultants at the time, was commissioned to design a new bridge and obtain all regulatory permits that were required for construction.
Anzac Contractors Inc. was awarded the construction contract in September 2004, and the project was completed at the cost of $3,447,288.58, two years later in October 2006. The new bridge was constructed using individually prestressed Sonovoid Units, which are held together by transverse post tensioning. The new bridge consists of a single structure that replaced two separate bridges, one for east-bound traffic and the other for west-bound traffic (Bridge numbers 875104 and 875105). The new bridge was assigned bridge number 875105 and bridge number 875104 was no longer required.
BACKGROUND
In 2019, the National Bridge Inventory (NBI) rating guidance for Sonovoid bridges was revised and resulted in a reduction in the sufficiency score for the West Relief Bridge. As a consequence, the FDOT Inspection report dated February 23, 2022, categorized the 16-year-old bridge as structurally deficient.
On May 11, 2022, then Town Manager Maria Lasday approved a proposal from BCC Engineering LLC (BCC) in the amount of $154,600 to first confirm the information in the FDOT inspection report and then prepare plans and specifications to repair the bridge. To confirm the findings in the FDOT report, BCC commissioned a Life Cycle Cost Analysis (LCCA) and a Chloride Analysis. Based on these analyses it was recommended that the bridge should be rehabilitated and end spans (spans 1 and 5) needed to be replaced. Furthermore, it was concluded that there was no economic advantage in replacing the entire bridge.
Of the $154,600, $103,602 was spent on the LCCA and Chloride analyses, and completion of 40% design plans.
BCC is one of the CCNA consultants who are currently on contract with the Town to provide general Civil Engineering services.
DISCUSSION
Originally, designs to rehabilitate the bridge and replace spans 1 and 5 were budgeted in fiscal 2024-25.
In October 2024, Town Engineer R. L. Daniel suggested to then Town Manager Rosado that this project be reprioritized to fiscal years 2025-26 and 2026-27, for design and construction respectively, for the following reasons:
The term “structurally deficient” in the FDOT report means that FDOT believes that the bridge should undergo a series of repairs or replacement within six (6) years. The attached “Bridge Condition Terminology” narrative used by FDOT, defines “structurally deficient”.
FDOT did not request that a weight restriction be imposed for the bridge.
As a consequence of (1) and (2) the current structure continues to be safe for all legal vehicular loads.
The structurally deficient spans were being replaced so prevention of further deterioration was not a key objective.
Remaining useful life existed in the two spans that were earmarked to be replaced.
According to the FDOT definition of “structural deficient”, span replacements are required to be completed six years from the date of the first report in 2022 that categorized the bridge as structurally deficient, or by 2028. Notwithstanding reprioritization, replacement of spans 1 and 5 is on track for 100% construction completion in 2026-27, which is one year earlier than the 2028 due date.
The 2025-26 budget included an allocation of $100,000 to design the replacement spans. Permitting, bid support and CEI services were added to the project scope and a proposal from BCC was submitted in the amount of $553,399.
The adopted FY26 budget includes $100,000 for this project. The project is expected to be completed over two fiscal years: $199,475 in FY26 and $353,924 in FY27. This item requests a budget increase of $99,475 to fully fund the FY26 portion. The remaining $353,924 will be budgeted in FY27.
A separate agenda item on this agenda (May 13, 2026, regular council meeting) requests authorization for the budget amendment.
title: Approval of a proposal from BCC Engineering LLC in the amount of $553,399 to complete design, permitting, bid support, and Construction Engineering Inspection (CEI) Services for Rehabilitation of the West Relief (Bridge # 875105). – Town Manager

RECOMMENDATION:
Discuss and consider a contract in favor of Hazen and Sawyer (Hazen) in the amount of $76,510, to provide engineering support associated with Cycle 3 SSES Phase 1 RFI and Phase 2 Regulatory Reporting to Miami Dade Department of Environmental Resources Management (DERM).
BACKGROUND:
Miami Dade Conty Code (MDCC) requires that Volume Sewer Customers (VSC) of the Miami Dade Water and Sewer Department (MDWSD) comply with the threshold for infiltration and Inflow (I/I) of 5,000 gallon per day-inch-mile (GPDIM). When Cycle 3 Phase 1 Sanitary Sewer Evaluation Survey (SSES) was submitted by Hazen to DERM on November 12, 2022, three (of the six) sewer sub basins in the Town of Bay Harbor Islands were found to be out of compliance. In conjunction with the Public Works Department, a corrective action plan (CAP) was developed by Hazen to bring these basins into compliance.
DERM also indicated that the Phase 1 report was deemed to be incomplete, for all the VSC submittals. The fee associated with this agenda item is to provide two deliverables: (1) Respond to DERM’S RFI regarding the Phase 1 Report, and (2) Submit the Cycle 3 Phase 2 SSES Report.
DISCUSSION
Both the Cycle 3 Phase 2 Report and the response to DERM’s RFI are due by November 12, 2026. To show compliance with the 5,000 GPDIM threshold for all sub basins, DERM requires flow measurements during the wet season of June 1 to November 30, 2026. A prerequisite for flow measurements is the completion of projects that are expected to reduce I/I.
In September 2024 when the Town was under a Temporary Sewer Moratorium (TM), to encourage DERM to overturn the TM, the town committed to undertaking certain sewer improvement projects which were aimed at reducing I/I. The key projects consisted of installing T-liners, sewer manhole lining, installation of lockable sewer manhole covers for manholes located in valley gutter inverts, point repairs to sewer laterals, and the installation of missing sewer caps on sewer laterals.
All projects will be completed prior to retesting sewage flows that is expected to commence on June 1, 2026. Once preliminary results are available a meeting with DERM will be convened to ensure that the final SSES Phase 2 report meets all their requirements, before final submittal on November 12, 2026.

description:
BACKGROUNDThe Town’s Land Development Code currently contains strict numerical standards in Section 23-12(A). Property owners seeking relief from even minor numerical requirements must file a formal variance application before the Town Council, a process that can be time-consuming and administratively burdensome for both applicants and staff.
On April 22, 2026 the Town Council introduced the attached ordinance on first reading. The proposed ordinance is designed to provide limited, streamlined flexibility for single-family homeowners while preserving the Town’s ability to protect public health, safety, welfare, and neighborhood character.
During the drafting process, staff determined that a five (5) percentage point threshold is reasonable, as it provides meaningful relief for minor lot or building constraints without materially altering the intent of Section 23-12(A). Unlike a percentage-based reduction, a percentage-points approach allows the same absolute reduction regardless of the underlying numerical standard, providing greater predictability. The ordinance also explicitly preserves the variance process for any request that exceeds five percentage points or is disapproved by the Town Manager.
ANALYSIS
The attached ordinance makes the following key additions to the Town Code:
1. Creation of General Waiver Provisions (Article III, Chapter 2, Sec. 2-30 through 2-35): The ordinance establishes a new article that applies only to numerical requirements in the Land Development Code (not the Florida Building Code or other state/federal codes). This clarifies the limited scope of the waiver authority.
2. Town Manager Authority for Minor Numerical Waiver (Sec. 2-31):
a. Applicable only to single-family detached dwellings.
b. Waiver cannot exceed five (5) percentage points of the original requirement set forth in Section 23-12(A).
c. Conditions for approval include:
i. Written statement from applicant (extent, duration, reason);
ii. Written recommendation from Planning Division;
iii. Finding that reduction does not undermine public health, safety, welfare, nor negatively impact adjacent single-family properties.
d. Limitation: No cumulative reductions exceeding five (5) percentage points for the same parcel, regardless of multiple requests.
3. Disapproval – Variance Required (Sec. 2-32): If the Town Manager denies a waiver, the applicant may only seek relief through the Town Council variance process under Section 2-16. This ensures that more significant or contested requests still receive Council oversight.
4. Scope of Waiver (Sec. 2-33): Any approved waiver applies only to the specific lot and circumstances and is nontransferable.
5. Application Fee (Sec. 2-34): A non-refundable fee of $500 covers administrative costs, staff review, and the Planning Division’s written recommendation. No application is complete until the fee is paid.
6. Exclusions (Sec. 2-34 – duplicate numbering): The waiver does not apply to duplexes, townhouses, multi-family dwellings, vacant lots without an approved single-family home application, commercial/industrial/institutional uses, or the Florida Building Code.
CONCLUSION
This ordinance provides a measured, efficient administrative process for minor numerical waivers (up to five percentage points) from Section 23-12(A) for single-family detached dwellings. It reduces unnecessary variance applications, preserves Council oversight for disapprovals or larger requests, and includes clear safeguards for public health, safety, welfare, and adjacent properties. The $500 fee ensures cost recovery for staff review.
Approval of this ordinance will implement a streamlined waiver process consistent with the Town’s goal of efficient government while protecting neighborhood character.

RECOMMENDATIONS:
Ratification of 2nd emergency contract awarded to Florida Draw Bridges Inc. in the amount of $670,879.26, that was authorized by the Town Manager to perform emergency repairs at the Broad Causeway Intracoastal Waterway Bridge.
BACKGROUND
On December 19, 2025, FDOT informed the Town of Bay Harbor Islands by email that during a routine inspection of bridge # 875101 their inspectors noted deficiencies that required immediate repairs.
The emergency work that is associated with this email was awarded to FDI in the amount of $607,179.94 and ratified at the March 22 2026 regular council meeting.
On Thursday February 26, 2026, another email was sent by FDOT (copy enclosed) regarding new defects that were observed at the bridge # 875101. This email included photographs of concrete spalls and severe cracks with a statement of urgency for making the repairs. This memorandum addresses ratification of the emergency repair work that is associated with this FDOT email.
The temporary supports that were approved at the March 22, 2026, meeting were successfully installed by FDI.
DISCUSSION
Sections 2-1.2 and 2-1.3 in the Town Code outline the procedure for Emergency Procurements and are entitled “Exemptions and Waivers from competitive bidding” and “Emergency Procurements” respectively.
Due to the critical nature of the defects and the urgency expressed by FDOT, the Town Manager authorized the immediate award of the repair work under the emergency procurement guidelines. As required by the Town Code, we are formally notifying the Council of this emergency action at the next scheduled meeting (the April 22, 2026, regular council meeting) and request that the Council ratify this emergency procurement.
Work is expected to start on April 1, 2026, and both emergency repair contracts are expected to be completed in 15 weeks. FDI has agreed to increase assigned resources for these two emergency repair contracts and although the scope of work associated with the second emergency repair is about the same as the first, the contract time for the second was reduced by 50%.
The full extent of repairs that require urgent attention still has not been ascertained and additional emergency expenditures will likely be required. Staff will keep the Council apprised accordingly.

description:
Summary
This memo requests the formal adoption of a Reimbursement Resolution in connection with the proposed $75 Million Municipal Complex Project. Under IRS Treasury Regulation Section 1.150-2, the Town must formally declare its “Official Intent” to reimburse project-related costs paid from available funds prior to the issuance of tax-exempt bonds.Adoption of this resolution ensures that funds advanced by the Town for immediate needs—such as site preparation and architectural fees—can be replenished from bond proceeds once the permanent financing is secured.
Background & Funding Structure
The Town is moving forward with site preparation and planning of a new Municipal Complex. Given the scale and nature of the project, the primary funding mechanism is expected to be General Obligation (G.O.) Bonds, secured by the Town’s full faith and credit and repaid through the levy of ad valorem (property) taxes.
While G.O. Bonds are anticipated to serve as the principal financing vehicle, the Town is committed to pursuing a diversified funding approach that minimizes the burden on local property taxpayers. Staff will actively identify and apply for available state and federal grant programs, including but not limited to infrastructure grants, resilience and hazard mitigation funding, and any other intergovernmental aid the project may qualify for. To the extent grant funding is secured, the bond issue amount would be reduced accordingly.
Additionally, certain components of the Municipal Complex project are expected to include utility infrastructure improvements, such as sanitary sewer, stormwater, and water system upgrades. To the extent that project costs are attributable to utility infrastructure, the Town intends to recover the proportionate share of those costs through the applicable utility rate structure rather than through the G.O. Bond issuance. This approach ensures that utility-related capital costs are borne by rate-paying users in accordance with sound public finance principles, rather than being subsidized by the general ad valorem tax base.
Voter Approval Required
Under Article VII, Section 12 of the Florida Constitution, municipalities may issue bonds payable from ad valorem taxation and maturing more than twelve months after issuance only when approved by a vote of the electors who are freeholders (owners of real property not wholly exempt from taxation) within the Town. This specific franchise requirement means the Town must conduct a bond referendum limited to freeholder electors before the bonds can be issued.
Purpose of This Resolution
This resolution creates the required “paper trail” under federal tax law that allows the Town to reimburse itself from bond proceeds once the voters approve the issuance and the bonds are sold.
Preliminary Debt Service Outlook
The following estimates are provided for planning purposes only. The assumed interest rate is illustrative; actual rates will depend on market conditions and the Town’s credit rating at the time of sale. As of April 2026, AA-rated 30-year municipal bonds are trading in the range of approximately 4.50%–5.00%.

BACKGROUND
On October 7, 2024, FDOT informed the Town of Bay Harbor Islands by certified mail (copy enclosed) that the Bascule Spans (Movable Spans) of the Broad Causeway Intracoastal Waterway (ICWW) Bridge (Bridge # 875101) must be posted for weight restrictions as follows:
SU Trucks: 14 Tons
C Trucks: 19 Tons
ST5 Trucks: 25 tons
SU, C, and ST5 represent various categories of trucks. The typical weights of these truck types are illustrated in the attached “Truck Axle and Weight Configuration”. To give some perspective as to the severity of the weight restrictions, the maximum weights from the “Truck Axle and Weight Configurations” are 35 Tons for SU trucks and 40 Tons for C and ST5 trucks. Therefore, the current weight restrictions are about 50% of the standard truck weights.
In accordance with the FDOT letter, the ICWW Bridge was posted for the recommended weight restrictions on November 7, 2024, and remains posted to this date.
DISCUSSION
At the February 20, 2025, Regular Council meeting, Council approved Ardurra Group Inc working with Hardesty and Hanover LLP (Hardesty) to prepare construction plans to repair old Bridge # 875101. Although originally expected to be completed by October 2025, the plans were submitted on February 2, 2026. It is expected that the project to perform structural repairs will be advertised by the end of February 2026. The approved amount for the completed plans is $407,180.
At the 90% completion stage of the above-mentioned plans, additional deficiencies were discovered. Modification of the existing plans to cater to these defects would have delayed the entire project, and it was considered in the best interest of the Town to proceed with the repair plans based on the original scope of work. The additional deficiencies will be handled by a supplemental design task work order and, if approved, a change order will amend the original scope of work.
This supplemental request includes the development of Bridge Repair Plans for additional repair items associated with the bascule span operating machinery. These items represent deficiencies that were not reported in the FDOT District 6 Routine (01/19/2024) or Special (1/14/2025) Inspection Reports, which were used as the basis for developing the final repair plans that were submitted on 2/6/2026.
Based on the findings, these items were recommended by Hardesty for inclusion as a supplement to the repair plans, as addressing them will help ensure the reliable operation of the bascule span.
The additional mechanical repairs include the following:
Development of repair plans for all bearing supports with anchors exhibiting excessive section loss.
Design of hold-down clamp for three machinery bearing support assemblies, B-3, B-4 and B-5.
The hold down clamp repair is critical to prevent machinery gear disengagement, which could result in a free-fall condition.
In addition to performing the design effort for the additional defects ($54,525), the task work order also consists of Project Management and coordination meetings (Ardurra - $16,880), Procurement Support Services or bidding assistance (Hardesty - $12,640), and Post Design Services (Hardesty - $87,330), for a grand total of $171,375.

description:
The Town’s current solid waste and recycling collection agreement expires on March 31, 2026. This memorandum provides historical context regarding our relationship with the current provider, Coastal Waste & Recycling (Coastal), details two negotiated rate options from Coastal, and presents a new unsolicited proposal from Waste Pro. Based on a review of these options, staff recommends waiving competitive procurement requirements and awarding the new contract to Waste Pro, as their proposal provides the most favorable terms and pricing for the Town.
Background and Contract History
The Town has benefited significantly from the current agreement, which originated through a competitive solicitation (RFP-174) in 2017. At that time, the Town awarded the contract to World Waste Recycling. In 2019, the Town Council approved the assignment of this contract to Coastal following their acquisition of World Waste.
The 2017 solicitation resulted in highly favorable pricing that positioned Bay Harbor Islands as having some of the lowest solid waste rates in Miami-Dade County.
Because of this competitive starting point, even with annual Consumer Price Index (CPI) adjustments and disposal fee increases, our current residential rate of $20.59 per unit remains remarkably low compared to market standards. Our current agreement provides a high service level that exceeds many neighboring municipalities, including 3x per week solid waste collection, 2x per week recycling collection, and 1x per week bulk trash collection.
Recent Developments & Waste Pro Proposal
In the weeks prior to the February Council meeting, the Town initiated discussions with Waste Pro regarding the possibility of taking over the Town's collection services. Initially, Waste Pro declined to submit a proposal, citing the short notice required to successfully take over the route.
However, on the afternoon of February 11, 2026, Waste Pro submitted a formal unsolicited proposal. Along with this submission, Waste Pro notified us of their Senior Management's firm commitment to take whatever action is necessary to be fully operational and ready to begin servicing the Town starting April 1.
Rate Comparison
We have compiled the current rates, the two renewal options negotiated with Coastal, and the new proposal submitted by Waste Pro for comparison.Coastal Option 1 (Long-Term Competitive Stability): Expires March 2029. Provides budget predictability but requires a substantial rate increase.
Coastal Option 2 (Short-Term Flexibility): Expires September 2026. Places rates among the highest in the county but allows flexibility to explore long-term strategies.
Waste Pro Proposal: Offers a highly competitive rate structure across both residential and commercial services, presenting significant savings compared to both Coastal options.

description:
Proposed Action: Authorize the Town Manager to submit a formal notification letter to the Florida Department of Economic Opportunity (DEO) stating the Town’s determination that updates to its Comprehensive Plan are necessary.
Key Facts & Why This is Needed:
Mandatory 7-Year Review: State law requires local governments to periodically evaluate and update their Comprehensive Plans to reflect new state laws and local conditions.
Current Plan is Outdated: The Town’s core plan was adopted in 1989, with its Future Land Use Element last substantively updated in 2004. It does not include numerous modern state requirements.
Formal Notice of Non-Compliance: The DEO has formally notified the Town that it is non-compliant with a 2015 state law requiring a “Peril of Flood” component for coastal resilience. A full plan update is the state’s required path to resolve this.
Consequences of Inaction: Failure to update the plan leaves the Town vulnerable to legal challenges during development reviews and unable to efficiently address new state mandates.
Purpose of the Letter: This notification starts a one-year deadline for the Town to finalize, hold public hearings on, and adopt a fully updated and compliant Comprehensive Plan. The necessary draft plan, which includes all required updates, was prepared in 2018 and is ready for this final adoption process.
Bottom Line: This step is not discretionary; it is a required legal action to modernize the Town’s foundational planning document, resolve long-standing compliance issues, and provide clear, current guidance for the Town’s future.

Task 5: Post Design Services

Greater efficiency with responses to request for information (RFI) from the contractor.
Greater efficiency in the transition from the Construction phase to the startup and commissioning phase, that will be performed by KHA.
The cost to provide CEI Services will be lower from a consultant who performed the project design.

description:
Proposed Action: Authorize the Town Manager to submit a formal notification letter to the Florida Department of Economic Opportunity (DEO) stating the Town’s determination that updates to its Comprehensive Plan are necessary.
Key Facts & Why This is Needed:
Mandatory 7-Year Review: State law requires local governments to periodically evaluate and update their Comprehensive Plans to reflect new state laws and local conditions.
Current Plan is Outdated: The Town’s core plan was adopted in 1989, with its Future Land Use Element last substantively updated in 2004. It does not include numerous modern state requirements.
Formal Notice of Non-Compliance: The DEO has formally notified the Town that it is non-compliant with a 2015 state law requiring a “Peril of Flood” component for coastal resilience. A full plan update is the state’s required path to resolve this.
Consequences of Inaction: Failure to update the plan leaves the Town vulnerable to legal challenges during development reviews and unable to efficiently address new state mandates.
Purpose of the Letter: This notification starts a one-year deadline for the Town to finalize, hold public hearings on, and adopt a fully updated and compliant Comprehensive Plan. The necessary draft plan, which includes all required updates, was prepared in 2018 and is ready for this final adoption process. This step is not discretionary; it is a required legal action to modernize the Town’s foundational planning document, resolve long-standing compliance issues, and provide clear, current guidance for the Town’s future.

description:
OBJECTIVES
Design a new bridge to replace the existing Broad Causeway Intra Coastal Waterway Bridge (Bridge # 875101), which is a 75-year-old bridge over the Intra Coastal Waterway.
PREAMBLE
The Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) will oversee Federal and State grants in total amount of One Million Five Hundred Thousand Dollars ($1.5 M) to offset some of the design costs for the new Broad Causeway Intra Coastal Waterway Bridge. Of the total amount, $1.0 M is from State Funds and $0.5 M, is from Federal Funds.
The LAP Agreements provides the framework for the Town to comply with the requirements of the grants and to enable the Town to receive reimbursements up to full amounts of the State and Federal grants.
BACKGROUND
The Broad Causeway Intra Coastal Waterway Bridge was built in 1951 and because of its age, has been categorized as structurally deficient by FDOT, unsafe for non-motorized traffic, and has become extremely expensive to maintain to keep it open to all legal vehicular traffic loads. The bridge is currently posted for weight restrictions and must be replaced. The Town hired Atkin Realis to provide a PD&E study which is in the final stages of completion. The next step for the Town will be to hire a bridge design firm to design a new bridge and prepare a bid package to solicit construction bids to build the new bridge.
DISCUSSION
The Town has budgeted $15.0 M to design the bridge over the two fiscal years, $7.5 M per year. A Request for Qualifications (RFQ), that will be issued before the end of 2025, will solicit responses from Bridge Design Engineers to submit design proposals to build the new bridge.
title: Discussion and possible action to approve the FDOT LAP Agreement for the Broad Causeway ICWW Bridge Design. Sponsored by Town Manager Lindsley Noel.

description:
OBJECTIVES
Design a new bridge to replace the existing 67-year-old Bay Harbor Waterway Bridge (Bridge # 875102), over the Bay Harbor Waterway Canal.
PREAMBLE
The Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) will oversee Federal grants in the amount of $525,520 to offset some of the design costs for the new Bay Harbor Waterway Bridge (Bridge # 875102). The total cost of the design is $700,693 and the Town’s contribution is $175,173.
The LAP Agreements provides the framework for the Town to comply with the requirements of the grants and to enable the Town to receive reimbursements up to full amounts of the grant.
BACKGROUND
The Bay Harbor Waterway Bridge was built in 1958, and because of its age, has been categorized as structurally deficient by FDOT. In 2024 FDOT issued a National Bridge Inspection (NBI) rating of 4 for the bridge deck and superstructure. This rating translates to a “poor condition” of these structural elements. Any municipal bridge that receives an inspection rating below 5 (out of 10), is added to the Statewide Bridge Replacement list, thereby making it available for Federal and State Grant funding. This program has a federal funding cap of 75% on $5M contract, and the local municipality funds the remaining 25%.
Accordingly, the Bay Harbor Waterway Bridge (Bridge # 875102) was added to the Statewide Bridge Replacement list and funding has been assigned based on FDOT’s estimate of the design and construction costs.
Staff have reviewed these estimates and agree that they appear to be reasonable.
DISCUSSION
A Request for Qualifications (RFQ) will be issued before the end of 2025 and will solicit responses from Bridge Design Engineers to submit design qualifications/proposals to build the new bridge.

description:
OBJECTIVES
Maximize CRS credit points assigned to the Town to improve CRS ranking, and gain access to Federal funds for projects that improve resiliency to flooding and hurricanes.
BACKGROUND
The Town of Bay Harbor Islands participates in the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) and receives credit for improving the community’s resiliency to flooding through CRS credit points. CRS is the acronym for the Community Rating System. CRS points are credited for the Town’s adoption of the County’s LMS plan, which contains the County’s Floodplain Management Plan The other advantage of adopting the County’s LMS Plan is to gain access to Federal funds for the Town’s flood and storm-related projects, whenever funds are assigned based on prior impact of hurricanes on the region.
The Town last adopted the County’s LMS plan in September 2020. The LMS Plan is revised every five years.
DISCUSSION
The Florida Division of Emergency Management has approved the Miami-Dade County 2025 Local Mitigation Strategy Plan pending adoption. Approval is granted when all technical components of the plan have been met. However, to be fully approved, each jurisdiction within Miami-Dade County must adopt the plan through their own governing body. Having an approved hazard mitigation plan is a requirement to participate in FEMA Hazard Mitigation Assistance (HMA) programs such as the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP).

attachments.name: Ordinance relating to Sec. 23-5 Automobile Showrooms (BHI) 2ND READING

description:
For over 20 years, the Town of Bay Harbor Islands was home to a long-standing automobile dealership that served the surrounding community. When the Town updated many of its original Land Development Regulations (LDRs) approximately two decades ago, automobile dealerships were removed as a permitted use in the Code. The existing dealership at that time was grandfathered in but eventually closed. While no specific site was initially proposed for this use, the topic has resurfaced due to renewed business interest.
On February 20, 2025, the Town Council unanimously approved an ordinance on second reading (7-0 vote) to prohibit the sale, leasing, rental, display, or repair of automobiles, trucks, boats, trailers, or recreational vehicles within the B-1 Business District. This action was intended to preserve the walkable, mixed-use character of the district and to avoid the impacts associated with traditional automobile-related uses.
However, seven months later, the Town Council expressed a shift in policy direction. In light of interest from high-end, low-impact automotive retailers, Council members indicated a willingness to allow automobile showrooms, but strictly limited to the sale, leasing, and display of vehicles—excluding any repair, maintenance, or service operations. These showrooms are intended to function as boutique-style, appointment-based spaces, consistent with the Town’s commercial aesthetic.
On first reading of the proposed ordinance, the Town Council voted 6-0 to advance the measure to second reading. During that meeting, representatives from Aston Martin, the prospective operator of a future showroom, provided interior renderings and conceptual images of the proposed build-out. These images reflected a high-end, gallery-like showroom environment, fully enclosed and consistent with the proposed zoning criteria.
The attached ordinance reflects the Council’s current direction, establishing a new "Automobile Showroom" use in the B-1 Business District with clearly defined regulations to limit potential impacts and preserve the district's character.
title: Consideration and approval of an Ordinance on Second Reading Amending Section 23-5 of the Town Code for the B-1 Business District to remove automobile showrooms for display and sales from the list of prohibited uses, thereby allowing them as a permitted use. Sponsored by Vice Mayor Stephanie Bruder.

description:
The Town of Bay Harbor Islands seeks to strengthen its oversight of new construction and site development by ensuring that all projects meet required setbacks, grading, and drainage standards from the outset. To support this goal, the Town is implementing clearer and more enforceable survey requirements that allow any errors to be identified and corrected early in the construction process, before they result in costly conflicts or code violations. Currently, the Florida Building Code requires a spot survey and a final survey, which are reviewed solely by the Building Official. However, these surveys are not addressed in the Town Code and are not reviewed by the Town Planner or Town Engineer. This gap in oversight has occasionally led to the construction of noncompliant features.
By incorporating specific survey requirements into the Planning and Zoning Code, and by requiring cross-departmental review, the Town will be better equipped to verify compliance throughout all stages of development. This approach will improve quality control, support better enforcement, and build public confidence that all development is proceeding in accordance with approved plans and Town regulations.

attachments.name: BHI Ordinance relating to expiration of development permits 2nd Reading

description:
The proposed ordinance establishes clear timelines and progress requirements for active building permits in the Town of Bay Harbor Islands. It is intended to prevent long-term inactivity, known as "permit squatting," which can lead to aesthetic deterioration, safety hazards, and negative impacts on surrounding property values.
Key features include:
Permits expire after 180 days of inactivity unless substantial progress is demonstrated.
Only one 90-day administrative extension may be granted by the Building Official.
Statutory extensions under state law are honored but require formal documentation.
Enforcement tools include stop work orders, fines, liens, and potential denial of future permits for repeat offenders.
The ordinance introduces a $10,000 cash bond requirement for at-risk or inactive projects.
A structured appeal process allows permit holders to challenge enforcement actions.
This ordinance enhances the Town’s ability to ensure timely completion of construction projects and maintain community standards.

description:
At a Special Council Meeting held on July 29, 2025, the Town Council adopted a resolution establishing a tentative millage rate of 3.4583 mills for Fiscal Year 2025–2026. This rate exceeds the rolled-back rate of 2.9836 mills. Based on the Town’s overall gross taxable value, which includes $266,204,561 in new construction added to the tax roll, the adopted tentative millage rate is projected to generate approximately $1,438,803 in additional property tax revenue compared to the prior fiscal year.

Attached is the Town Manager’s memorandum to the Council recommending the Fiscal Year 2026 property tax rate of 3.4583 mills per $1,000 of taxable value. For comparison, the “rolled-back” rate is 2.9836 mills, meaning the proposed rate represents a 15.91% increase over the rolled-back rate.

description:
The FY 2026 proposed budget includes an increase in the Town’s general operating millage rate from 3.1728 to 3.4583 mills, which exceeds the rolled-back rate of 2.9836 mills. Based on the Town’s overall gross taxable value, which includes $266,204,561 in new construction added to the tax roll, the adopted tentative millage rate is projected to generate approximately $1,438,803 in additional property tax revenue compared to the prior fiscal year.
As reported by the Miami-Dade County Property Appraiser on July 1, 2025, the 2025 Taxable Value for the Town is $2,346,469,213, reflecting an increase of $266,204,561 over the 2024 final certified taxable value of $2,080,264,652. This growth is primarily driven by new development and construction activity, which has significantly expanded and diversified the Town’s tax base.
The enhanced property valuations strengthen the Town’s financial foundation, enabling continued investment in the community. These resources will help address growing service demands—including expanded recreational programming, updated equipment and facilities, and infrastructure improvements—while also supporting initiatives to attract new businesses and enhance overall quality of life.
While broader economic conditions continue to exert pressure on other revenue streams, the Town remains in a stable financial position. The FY 2026 budget reflects a disciplined approach to fiscal management, with a continued commitment to maintaining adequate reserves, supporting long-term financial goals, and planning for sustainable growth and development.
The total net operating budget for FY 2026 is $54,047,919, which is $2,034,653 more than the FY 2025 adopted net operating budget, due to cost of living increases and capital infrastructure projects. The FY 2026 budget will require appropriations from Fund Balance reserves in the Enterprise Funds.
Personnel ServicesPersonnel Services costs represent 30.23% of the total budget and 59.15% of the General Fund budget. The funded General employee compensation projections are based on a 2% to 5% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA), and a 2.5% to 5% (Merit) based on the employee’s Collective Bargaining Agreements. The CBA contract with Law Enforcement was executed during FY 2024 and is valid through September 30, 2026. The CBA contract with the American Federation of State County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME) was executed during FY 2024 and is valid through September 30, 2026. Pension contributions were projected using the estimated rates calculated by the Town Actuary, for General employees 19.45%, and Police Officers 24.62%.
The staffing additions, revisions, and deletions are:Eliminated the Administrative/Operations Manager position.
Restored funding for one (1) full-time Executive Assistant to the Town Manager position.
Restored funding for one (1) full-time Assistant Finance Director position.
Restored funding for one (1) full-time Electrician position.
Eliminated one (1) full-time Accounting Manager position.
Eliminated one (1) full-time IT Technician.
Eliminated the Community Service and Event Coordinator.
Reclassified the IT Director to an IT Manager Position.
Reinstated the Office Pass Plan position as a full-time Administrative Services Specialist.
Reclassified the Business Development Specialist position to Administrative Services Supervisor.
Reclassified the Customer Service Specialist position to Administrative Services Specialist.
Added one (1) full-time Public Service Aide.
Added one (1) full-time Accreditation Manager.
Added one (1) part-time Police Property Records Specialist.
Eliminated one (1) full-time Dispatcher position.
Added one (1) part-time Crossing Guard.
Added one (1) full-time Parks and Recreation Director.
Added one (1) full-time Assistant Parks and Recreation Director.
Added one (1) part-time Park Ranger.
Reclassified the Project Manager position to Capital Improvements Director.
The reclassification and additional positions are in the Town Manager’s, Finance, Public Works, Community Services Programming, Parks and Recreation, and Law Enforcement departments to support and enhance the operational needs and public safety operations.
General Fund
General Fund revenues and expenditures for FY 2026 are $14,506,012, a net increase of $1,968,632, or 15.70% from FY 2025.
In addition to the staffing changes above, the FY 2026 General Fund budget includes funds for the following:
Support for Sister Cities.
Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Cameras.
Additional allocation for travel and training expenditures for all employees.
Continue to enhance operations by investing in technology associated with advancement in software for operations.
Continue the funding for the Bright Paths Youth Development program funded partially by the Children’s Trust.
Continue the funding for the Annual Art Festival.
Leased warehouse space to serve as a storage facility and designated Emergency Operations Center (EOC) location.
LED stop signs.
The budget includes capital projects in FY 2026 that would require a transfer of $300,000 from the Building Fund to the Capital Projects Fund for the Town Hall Project. Capital Outlay for Public Safety and Parks Improvements is accounted for in the Capital Projects Fund, instead of the General Fund and is funded with interest income and appropriation of fund balance.
Capital Outlay and Capital Projects Fund
Capital Outlay and Capital Improvements Projects can affect the Town’s operating budget by increasing expenditures and being offset by projected savings or new revenues generated by the project. In FY 2026, the Town will invest a total of $19,688,198 in capital, 54% in improvements other than buildings (bridge replacement and repairs), 10% in Town Hall Project, 10%, Parking Fund 6.95%, in Sewer projects, 6% in Water projects, 8% in Stormwater projects, 2% in Machinery and Equipment, 3% in vehicles and 0.5% in computer software.
Enterprise Funds:
Causeway Fund
The Town of Bay Harbor Islands FY 2026 adopted budget for the Causeway Fund will fund capital outlay improvement projects.
Since the engineering report on the Town’s four owned bridges determined that the main Causeway Bridge is functionally obsolete, the Causeway Bridge needs to be replaced. The Causeway Bridge project is currently in the final stages of the Project Design and Environmental (PD&E) process and will be proceeding with the design phase in FY 2026.
During FY 2022, the Town issued a Request for Qualifications and received proposals from five (5) engineering firms to assist with the Broad Causeway Bridge replacement project. The selection committee reviewed proposals from these engineering companies and after long consideration concluded that Atkins North America, Inc. would be the best suitable for the BC-160 Broad Causeway Drawbridge Replacement project. Since then, the Town amended its FY 2022 annual budget and fully funded the Project Design and Environmental (PD&E) Study stage in FY 2022 with a completion date running to FY 2026. The advancement of PD&E funding was needed due to Miami-Dade County LRTP/TIP requirements regarding the application entry to TPO programming. For FY 2026, the Town has allocated $15 million of Causeway funds to fund the design for the Broad Causeway Bridge Replacement Project. The appropriations that are not expended in the FY 2026 budget year will be carried forward to the FY 2027 budget year. The Town will continue to actively pursue grants and appropriations for this project.
The said engineering report also stated that the Indian Creek and West Relief bridges were structurally deficient. As a result, weight limits were imposed by the Federal Department of Transportation (FDOT). It is anticipated that with the full completion of the Indian Creek Bridge repairs, the weight restrictions may be lifted.
The other Causeway Fund capital outlay projects include appropriations for the following:
Waterway Bridge structural repairs (Middle Bridge) BC – 161
Artificial Reef Project funding for Phase I and Phase II
West Relief Bridge-N Miami Design & Construction
Sewer and Water Fund
A water rate increase of 2.81%, which represents a pass-through increase for our customers as a result of Miami-Dade County Water and Sewer Department’s rate increase for water purchased by the utility. The FY 2026 budget includes a rate increase for water service revenue projections.
The City of Miami Beach increased the surcharge to the County’s rates to determine the rates charged to the Town for wastewater removal. The Town analyzed the proposal from the City of Miami Beach for the surcharge increase and projected an increase of 26% to the wholesale sewer rate in FY 2026.
The Town is budgeting several additional capital outlay projects in Sewer and Water Funds.
Parking Fund
In FY 2026, parking revenues, including an increase in parking fees. The expenditures include partial funding for (1) Compliance Manager, (1) Parking and Crossing Guard Supervisor, (1) Parking Enforcement Officer, and operating expenses such as merchant fees, operating supplies, repairs & maintenance of equipment and other recurring charges.
Notable Parking Fund capital outlay expenditures that are budgeted in Fiscal Year 2026 are below:
BHI-248 New Town Hall Parking Lot Design.
Parking Meter Machine Software.
Solid Waste
In FY 2026, service revenues for the monthly solid waste collection fee for residents and businesses are projected to be stagnant. Although Coastal Waste and Recycling increased the pickup fees by approximately 2.9% as allowed by contract, the Town has adjusted the revenues during the budget year, which includes a built-in CPI adjustment.
Stormwater FundIn FY 2026, the Stormwater budget is increasing due to funding for BHI-238 West Bay Harbor Stormwater improvement project.
Millage Recommendation
The recommended millage rate for Fiscal Year 2026 is 3.4583 mills, compared to the rolled-back rate of 2.9836 mills. This rate is based on a certified 12.8% increase in the Town’s overall taxable value, as reported by the Miami-Dade County Property Appraiser on July 1, 2025.
The certified gross taxable value increased by approximately $266 million, resulting in an estimated $1,387,026 in additional property tax revenue over the prior year. The total amount of taxes to be levied is $7,709,055.
At a 95% collection rate, the millage rate of 3.4583 mills is projected to generate $7,709,055 in budgeted property tax revenue for FY 2026, based on a total tax levy of $8,114,794.
The Town of Bay Harbor Islands has experienced solid growth in taxable property value in recent years; 9.7% in FY 2025, and 12.8% in FY 2026.
The Town Council and dedicated staff have worked hard to develop this year’s budget so that the Town can continue to provide extensive, quality services, amenities, and infrastructure that improve and beautify the Town, address safety, and provide financial stability for the Town’s residents and property owners.
We have developed a budget that positions the Town to remain competitive in the employment market, recognizing that recruiting and retaining qualified personnel is essential to maintaining the high quality of life our residents expect and deserve. Fiscal responsibility remains a core value shared by the entire management team and is reflected throughout this budget.
We are fortunate to have a dedicated and resilient staff who continue to deliver exceptional service without interruption. Their commitment ensures that operations run smoothly and residents receive the highest level of service.
This budget is conservative in its revenue projections and lean in expenditures, reflecting a disciplined approach to financial planning. Our goal is to align available resources with the Town Council’s priorities and strategic goals, and we remain optimistic about our ability to meet those expectations while upholding the Town’s strong fiscal standing.
I continue to express my gratitude for the commitment, energy, and contribution of the elected officials and the staff members who continue to deliver a high level of service to the Town of Bay Harbor Islands community.

description:
BACKGROUND
The Town of Bay Harbor Islands has participated in the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) since 1972. The Town is currently a Class 9 CRS community and as a result all policyholders are rewarded with a 5% reduction in their flood insurance premiums. Raising the Town’s CRS ranking would increase the discount on flood insurance policies.
The Flood Insurance Assessment (FIA) is part of the Town of Bay Harbor Islands floodplain management program under the CRS. The FIA uses data from flood insurance policies and past paid claims, to determine the number of properties with flood insurance coverage.
DISCUSSION
Based on the data collected, approximately half of the properties in the Town do not have flood insurance. All buildings in the town are located within the Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA) and are therefore at risk of flooding.
The FIA concluded that about half of the Town’s residents were renters who would rely on contents coverage in the event of flood damage and should be encouraged to purchase insurance to cover the contents of their rental units.
title: Flood Insurance Assessment Report. Sponsored by Town Manager Lindsley Noel.

description:
OBJECTIVE
Maximize Community Rating System (CRS) credit points assigned to the Town to provide our residents with larger discounts for flood insurance.
BACKGROUND
The Town of Bay Harbor Islands has participated in the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) since 1972. The Town is currently a Class 9 CRS community and as a result all policyholders are rewarded with a 5% reduction in their flood insurance premiums. Repetitive loss may be defined as any insurable building for which two or more claims of more than $1,000 were paid by the NFIP within any rolling 10-year period, since 1978.
To receive credit, the Repetitive Loss Area Analysis (RLAA) must be submitted to the Town Council and adopted. It must also be made available to the media and the public.
DISCUSSION
According to data provided by FEMA dated September 2, 2024, the Town of Bay Harbor Islands has five repetitive loss properties. By virtue of the number of RL properties the Town is a Category B repetitive loss community. (Category A, 0 repetitive loss properties, Category B, 1 -50 repetitive loss properties, and Category C greater than 50 repetitive loss properties).
Category B repetitive loss communities are required by CRS to research and describe their repetitive loss, create a map showing the location of all repetitive loss properties and complete an annual outreach activity directed to repetitive loss properties. For a detailed evaluation of repetitive loss, the Town opted to complete a Repetitive Loss Area Analysis (RLAA) using the 2017 CRS Coordinator’s Manual. The RLAA also benefits the Town by examining potential mitigation measures and increases the Town’s credit in the CRS program.
title: A Resolution to approve/adopt the Repetitive Loss Area Analysis (RLAA) for the Town. Sponsored by Town Manager Lindsley Noel.

description:
On June 11, 2025, the Town Council approved the first reading of the proposed ordinance (6-1 vote), allowing the item to proceed to second reading.
Following the first reading, no changes have been made to the draft language since the first reading.
Second-Story Restrictions in the RD District:
In 2023, the Town Council adopted ordinance revisions to discourage oversized single-family home development on the West Island, located within the RD district. These changes introduced second-story building area limitations to reduce visual massing and protect the architectural character of the neighborhood.
Although the Code permits applicants to request waivers from these restrictions, the authority to grant such waivers rests solely with the Town Council. The proposed amendment to Section 23-11 reinforces this by explicitly stating that the DRB shall not review or approve any floor plans associated with second-story waiver requests. This clarification removes ambiguity and ensures that all such waivers are considered only through the formal Town Council process.
Garage Area Limitations in the RD District:
In conjunction with second-story limits, the proposed amendments establish a new regulation for garage development in the RD district. Specifically, the total enclosed area of any garage shall not exceed 30 percent of the gross floor area of the first (ground) floor of the main residence, as measured inside exterior walls. This standard applies to all garage space, including both attached and detached structures, and includes both air-conditioned and non-air-conditioned garages.
This limitation is intended to prevent the construction of disproportionately large garage structures and to promote residential designs that reflect the intended scale and character of the RD zoning district.
title: Consideration and approval of an Ordinance on Second Reading amending Section 23-11 of the Town Code related to the second-story building area waivers and garage percentage in the RD District. Sponsored by Vice Mayor Stephanie Bruder.

attachments.name: Staff Memo for Council Agenda Items Automobile showroom 2nd Reading
Ordinance relating to Sec. 23-5 Automobile Showrooms (BHI) 2ND READING

description:
For over 20 years, the Town of Bay Harbor Islands was home to a long-standing automobile dealership that served the surrounding community. When the Town updated many of its original Land Development Regulations (LDRs) approximately two decades ago, automobile dealerships were removed as a permitted use in the Code. The existing dealership at that time was grandfathered in but eventually closed. While no specific site was initially proposed for this use, the topic has resurfaced due to renewed business interest.
On February 20, 2025, the Town Council unanimously approved an ordinance on second reading (7-0 vote) to prohibit the sale, leasing, rental, display, or repair of automobiles, trucks, boats, trailers, or recreational vehicles within the B-1 Business District. This action was intended to preserve the walkable, mixed-use character of the district and to avoid the impacts associated with traditional automobile-related uses.
However, seven months later, the Town Council expressed a shift in policy direction. In light of interest from high-end, low-impact automotive retailers, Council members indicated a willingness to allow automobile showrooms, but strictly limited to the sale, leasing, and display of vehicles—excluding any repair, maintenance, or service operations. These showrooms are intended to function as boutique-style, appointment-based spaces, consistent with the Town’s commercial aesthetic.
On first reading of the proposed ordinance, the Town Council voted 6-0 to advance the measure to second reading. During that meeting, representatives from Aston Martin, the prospective operator of a future showroom, provided interior renderings and conceptual images of the proposed build-out. These images reflected a high-end, gallery-like showroom environment, fully enclosed and consistent with the proposed zoning criteria.
The attached ordinance reflects the Council’s current direction, establishing a new "Automobile Showroom" use in the B-1 Business District with clearly defined regulations to limit potential impacts and preserve the district's character.
title: Consideration and approval of an Ordinance on Second Reading Amending Section 23-5 of the Town Code for the B-1 Business District to remove automobile showrooms for display and sales from the list of prohibited uses, thereby allowing them as a permitted use. Staff Memo for Council Agenda Items Required Survey 9.11 1ST READING

description:
The Town of Bay Harbor Islands seeks to strengthen its oversight of new construction and site development by ensuring that all projects meet required setbacks, grading, and drainage standards from the outset. To support this goal, the Town is implementing clearer and more enforceable survey requirements that allow any errors to be identified and corrected early in the construction process, before they result in costly conflicts or code violations. Currently, the Florida Building Code requires a spot survey and a final survey, which are reviewed solely by the Building Official. However, these surveys are not addressed in the Town Code and are not reviewed by the Town Planner or Town Engineer. This gap in oversight has occasionally led to the construction of noncompliant features.
By incorporating specific survey requirements into the Planning and Zoning Code, and by requiring cross-departmental review, the Town will be better equipped to verify compliance throughout all stages of development. This approach will improve quality control, support better enforcement, and build public confidence that all development is proceeding in accordance with approved plans and Town regulations.
title: Consideration and approval of an Ordinance on First Reading Amending Section 23-80 of the Town Code for to establish survey requirements for new construction, additions, and site modifications. Sponsored by Vice Mayor Stephanie Bruder.

attachments.name: Staff Memo for Council Agenda Items off-site parking 1st reading

description:
The Town has experienced ongoing issues related to construction worker parking throughout the community. Despite existing requirements for construction staging plans, including designated parking locations for all workers, numerous construction projects have failed to adequately manage off-site parking. Workers have been observed parking inappropriately throughout the Town, including in residents’ reserved parking spaces, along public rights-of-way, and in other unauthorized areas.
While the code currently allows the Town to review and approve staging plans, including worker parking arrangements, enforcement has become increasingly difficult. The uncontrolled nature of off-site parking has caused significant disruption to residents and local businesses. In response, the Town is considering a code amendment to prohibit all off-site construction worker parking within Town limits.
title: Consideration and approval of an Ordinance on first reading regarding construction parking. Sponsored by Vice Mayor Stephanie Bruder and Council Member Robert Yaffe.

description:
Recent Legislation – Senate Bill 180 (2025)
Florida has enacted Senate Bill 180, which establishes statewide standards for crane and hoisting equipment operations during hurricane season. Key requirements include:
Crane Securing Protocol (24 hours before storm):
Tower cranes must be placed in a weathervane position
Mobile cranes must retract booms, remove rigging, and secure counterweights
All equipment must follow manufacturer hurricane procedures
Hurricane Preparedness Plan:
Every site utilizing a crane must maintain an on-site written preparedness plan
This plan must be made available for inspection by state or local authorities
Enforcement:
Non-compliance may result in disciplinary action, including license suspension
​
Proposed Legislation – SB 346 / HB 6009
These bills seek to repeal Florida Statute 489.113(11), which currently preempts municipalities from regulating cranes and hoisting equipment. If passed, local governments would:
Regain the authority to adopt local ordinances governing crane use
Have discretion to regulate hurricane-related crane operations
Potentially require local crane permits or site-specific safety plans
Current Preemption Status
As it stands:
Municipalities cannot enforce their own crane-related safety standards, including storm preparations.
All regulatory authority rests with the state.
Implications for Our Town
If SB 346/HB 6009 passes:
We may consider drafting local ordinances or permit processes for crane operations, especially for active construction during hurricane season.
We may also need to prepare to coordinate local inspections and enforce preparedness plans.
Verdict
As of today, SB 346/HB 6009 did not pass the 2025 legislative session. We remain governed solely by SB 180 and state-level protocols.
